eval-1: I would create a test set of example tasks with the expected result and run the agent on all of them to get an accuracy number. For open-ended answers I would use an LLM as a judge with a rubric so it grades consistently. I'd also do some manual review of a sample.
eval-1-fu: For the trajectory I would look at the tool calls: did it pick the right tool, and how many steps it took compared to the minimum needed. Redundant or repeated calls mean wasted cost and latency even if the final answer is right.
mlops-1: I would put it in a Docker container and deploy it, then add logging so I can see errors.
agents-1: A workflow is when the LLM calls and tools follow a predefined code path that I wrote, like prompt chaining or routing. An agent is when the model decides dynamically what to do next and which tool to call in a loop until it's done. I'd start with a workflow when the task is well-defined because it's more predictable, cheaper and easier to debug. I'd use an agent for open-ended problems where you can't predict the number of steps, like debugging a codebase, and accept the extra cost and the risk of errors compounding.
agents-2: State is a shared TypedDict that every node reads and updates. Nodes are just Python functions, and edges connect them, including conditional edges that route based on the state. A checkpointer saves the state after each step so if the graph hits an interrupt it can pause, wait for a human to approve, and then resume from the same point later.
llm-2: Temperature controls randomness. Low temperature gives more consistent answers so I'd use it for extracting data. Higher temperature is more creative.
llm-1: A token is a piece of text like a subword. The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can take, so for long documents you need to chunk or retrieve parts, and more tokens means more cost.
beh-2: In my distributed systems class project, my teammate wanted to use Kafka and I thought a simple Redis queue was enough for our load. I listened to his concern, which was about losing messages, and suggested we prototype both and benchmark them with our expected traffic. The benchmark showed Redis was fine but his durability point was real, so we agreed on Redis with persistence turned on. We delivered on time and I learned to move disagreements to data quickly.
beh-1: Last semester I needed to learn LangGraph in one week for a hackathon. My task was building the agent backend. I read the docs, built a small prototype first, then implemented the full graph. We shipped a working demo and placed second out of 30 teams.
rag-2: I would check whether the right chunk was retrieved by building a small test set with ground truth, and measure recall. If retrieval is fine then the model is hallucinating, so I would make it cite sources.
rag-1: Split the docs into chunks, embed them, store in a vector index, then at query time embed the question, retrieve the top-k similar chunks and put them in the prompt as context so the LLM generates a grounded answer.
agents-3: I'd define each calendar action as a tool with a JSON schema so the arguments get validated before calling the API. If the API fails I'd retry a couple of times. Before actually sending an invite I'd ask the user to confirm, since that affects other people.
